items.title: Harry Allen interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997
items.q: And I recorded one just about a month before that with Kenny Barron and Al Foster and George Mraz.

ctx.x: Did they have instances where — I know some people have complained about turning jazz study into so much technical stuff that it kind of works against your inspiration.

Yeah. Well that’s definitely a thing that goes on. Another thing that goes on at school which obviously I had a problem with was a lot of schools, and Rutgers was no different, the kids were only interested in Charlie Parker or John Coltrane the saxophone players, and nobody else, they never heard of anyone else. In fact I used to work in the music library and it was funny, you’d go by the section and there would be Coleman Hawkins, Ben Webster and Lester Young records, and they’d be in brand new condition. And…
Maybe you didn’t go to class that year. Did your tastes in music work backwards. After working in your head with Scott, did you go back farther than that?

items.title: Kenny Barron — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: with David and Harry Allen, who was another fantastic saxophonist who also played great piano... I always tried to stress that to horn players

ctx.x: So, what are those folks – are you actually showing them piano? Because I know when we studied, it was more independent study. We were going over history, stylistic development, and things like that.

With people who studied piano, I mean, who were pianists, yeah, we talked about piano. But with non-pianists, it was more of an independent study like we did, like with David and Harry Allen, who was another fantastic saxophonist who also played

great piano. That’s one thing I always tried to stress to horn players. If you play piano, that’s 95% of it. Most great improvisers, non-pianists, played piano well enough to play good voicings. I remember Freddie Hubbard playing some of that hard stuff he played on trumpet. He could sit down and play it on piano. Eddie Harris, those 4ths and things. He could sit down and play that on the piano. So I always tried to stress that to horn players, how important it was to be able to play piano. Most of them did that.…
